notes.title: Chapter map: Performance & reliability
notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

This section is mostly arithmetic: Little's Law, the ρ / (1 − ρ) curve, fan-out 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ, retry amplification kⁿ. One idea runs through all of it: every failure here is a queue that was allowed to grow.

  • An unbounded call grows the in-flight queue.
  • An unbudgeted retry grows the arrival rate.
  • An unbounded buffer grows memory.
  • A shared pool lets one slow dependency fill everyone's queue.

The fixes are the same shape each time: bound it, budget it, or split it.

Concept map

Measurement comes first because every later note fixes one segment or one queue that measurement found.

Green holds a CORE note, blue is SUPPORTING; 153–154 holds one of each (153 CORE), and 147–148 and 149–150 are both CORE. There are no BREADTH items, so there's no breadth.md. Neighbours: timeouts, retries and backoff owns the HTTP contract and jitter strategies below 149 and 150; rollouts and inference LB apply these ideas in Kubernetes; metrics that matter comes after.

Reading order:where latency goespoolingqueueing theorytimeoutsretriesidempotencybreakers and sheddingtail latencyHOL blockingdegradationcascadescapacity

Queueing (152) is read third because Little's Law sizes the pool in 148 and the bulkheads in 151; idempotency (155) right after retries because a retried timeout is only safe with it.

Each idea is explained in full in one note. Other notes link to it and don't repeat it.

A dependency is failing or slow. What do I reach for? Ask in this order. The first "yes" decides.

  • One big idea: every failure here is a queue allowed to grow; bound it, budget it or split it.
  • Two most-confused pairs: timeout vs deadline (a per-hop duration vs a shared absolute time), and hedge vs retry (racing slowness vs replacing a failure).
  • Ten minutes before a tech discussion: say "L = λW"; say "ρ / (1 − ρ): 9× at 90 %"; say "1 − 0.99ⁿ: 63 % at 100"; say "kⁿ: 27 at three hops, 1.33 with budgets"; walk the dependency tree above.

notes.title: Where Latency Actually Goes — Five Segments, Five Owners, One curl -w
notes.html:
References

everything.curl.dev: write-out variables · RFC 8446: TLS 1.3, §2 protocol overview · MDN: Navigation and resource timings · Ilya Grigorik: High Performance Browser Networking, ch. 1

TL;DR

A request's latency is five segments, each with a different owner:

  • DNS: the resolver and its caches.
  • TCP connect: 1 RTT, set by distance.
  • TLS handshake: 1 RTT on TLS 1.3, 2 on TLS 1.2.
  • Server think time: your code, plus 1 RTT for the request to go and the first byte to return.
  • Transfer: size over bandwidth, shaped by congestion control.

curl -w splits them in one command. The usual finding: on a cold connection at real distances, setup dominates. Reusing connections beats optimising code, because halving think time saves milliseconds and removing two RTTs saves hundreds.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:time_namelookup (DNS)time_connect (+1 RTT TCP)time_appconnect (+1 RTT TLS 1.3)time_pretransfertime_starttransfer (+1 RTT + think)time_total (+ transfer)

Recall

Prompt Answer
The five segments, in order? DNS → TCP connect → TLS → server think time → transfer.
Which curl subtraction isolates the wait for the server? time_starttransfer − time_pretransfer = think time + 1 RTT.
RTTs before the first request byte, cold, TLS 1.3? 2: one for TCP, one for TLS (TLS 1.2 needed 3).
What does a warm connection remove? DNS, TCP and TLS: all of setup.
High connect, everything else low? Distance or a congested path, not the app.
Draw by hand: a cold HTTPS request a timeline with five coloured bars, labelled DNS, TCP (1 RTT), TLS (1 RTT), wait (1 RTT + think), transfer; under it the warm version with only the last two.

The idea

A team in Mumbai calls a payments API in Virginia (about 150 ms RTT) and measures 520 ms per call. They profile the handler, cut its 40 ms of work to 20 ms, and ship. Latency drops to 500 ms: 4 %. The other 480 ms were never theirs to optimise in code. DNS, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake and the request's own round trip cost 4 × 150 ms + DNS on every cold call.

Measured first, the fix is obvious: reuse the connection, and three of the five segments disappear.

The trade: splitting latency by segment tells you which owner can fix it, and you pay only with one command per investigation, but you must resist optimising the segment you own because it's the one you can see.

How it works

One cold HTTPS call: four round trips before the body arrives.

The budget for one cold HTTPS call, from the formula below.

Segment curl subtraction Cost Owner Fix
DNS time_namelookup < 1 ms cached, 10–50 ms cold resolver, caches cache, longer TTL, ndots
TCP connect − namelookup 1 RTT distance reuse, move closer, edge termination
TLS appconnect − connect 1 RTT (1.3), 2 (1.2) protocol, resumption reuse, TLS 1.3, resumption
Wait starttransfer − pretransfer 1 RTT + think your code, plus distance code, caching, queueing
Transfer total − starttransfer size ÷ throughput bandwidth, congestion window compression, smaller payloads 
cold  = DNS + RTT (TCP) + RTT (TLS 1.3) + RTT (request) + think + transfer
warm  =                                   RTT (request) + think + transfer
150 ms RTT, 30 ms DNS, 40 ms think: cold = 30 + 150 + 150 + 150 + 40 = 520 ms · warm = 190 ms

Evolution

Lineage:1996 HTTP/1.0, a connection per request1997 HTTP/1.1 keep-alive2012 Navigation Timing in browsers2015 HTTP/2 multiplexingAug 2018 TLS 1.3 (1-RTT handshake)2022 HTTP/3 merges transport and TLS setup
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: HTTP/3 does transport and TLS in one RTT; curl 8 adds time_posttransfer and time_queue.
  • What won't change: each handshake costs round trips, and distance sets the RTT.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (curl 8.7.1, Python 3.15 HTTPS server with a 120 ms handler and a 200 kB body). Two URLs in one curl, so the second reuses the connection:

curl -s -o /dev/null -o /dev/null --cacert c.pem \
  -w 'dns %{time_namelookup} connect %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} pre %{time_pretransfer} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n' \
  https://localhost:8443/a https://localhost:8443/b
# dns 0.000022  connect 0.000458  tls 0.003436  pre 0.003476  ttfb 0.130058  total 0.134144   ← cold
# dns 0.000021  connect 0.000000  tls 0.000000  pre 0.000054  ttfb 0.125785  total 0.130648   ← reused
# the default that bites: the times are CUMULATIVE timestamps, not durations;
# reading "ttfb 0.130" as server time double-counts setup. Subtract.

On localhost the RTT is ~0.05 ms, so the server's 120 ms dominates. At 150 ms RTT, the same subtraction shows setup dominating instead.

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): what halving server work buys, against reusing the connection.

def latency(rtt, think, dns=30, cold=True):
    return (dns + 2 * rtt if cold else 0) + rtt + think
for rtt in (20, 150):
    print(rtt, latency(rtt, 40), latency(rtt, 20), latency(rtt, 40, cold=False))
# look for: the 150 ms row
# naive belief predicts: halving think time halves latency

Run: at 20 ms RTT, cold 130 ms; halving think saves 20 ms (15 %), reuse saves 70 ms (54 %). At 150 ms RTT, cold 520 ms; halving think saves 20 ms (4 %), reuse saves 330 ms (63 %).

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w with the five timestamps against the real endpoint, from where the caller runs; run it twice in one command to see warm.
  • In production: client-side spans split into DNS, connect, TLS and wait (OpenTelemetry HTTP client instrumentation records these); connection reuse ratio per client; browser Resource Timing for real users.
  • Bounded by: connection reuse → pooling and keep-alive; the think segment's queueing → queueing theory.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Latency is five segments: DNS, TCP connect, TLS, server wait and transfer, each with a different owner. curl -w gives cumulative timestamps, so each segment is a subtraction. On a cold connection at real distance, setup is three to four RTTs, which usually dwarfs server time. So I measure first, and the first fix is almost always connection reuse, then moving the edge closer, and only then the code.

Q · Mechanism — Why is starttransfer − pretransfer not server time? pretransfer is when curl is about to send the request; starttransfer is when the first response byte arrives. Between them the request crosses the network, the server works, and the first byte comes back: one full RTT plus think time. On a 150 ms path a 40 ms handler shows as 190 ms. Subtract the RTT from connect − namelookup to get think time.

Q · Trade-off — Optimise the code or move the termination point? Code changes shrink only think time. An edge or regional termination point (CDN, a regional proxy with warm pooled connections to the origin) turns a long-RTT handshake into a short one and reuses the long hop. Code when think time is the biggest segment; edge and reuse when setup is.

Q · Failure — p50 is fine but p99 has a fixed ~1 s and ~3 s step. Why? Steps at fixed values mean timers, not work: a lost SYN waits for the initial retransmission timeout (1 s on Linux, then 3 s after doubling on older stacks); a dropped DNS query waits the resolver's 5 s timeout. curl -w on slow samples puts the step in connect or namelookup, not in the wait. Fix the path loss or the resolver, not the code.

Q · Design — A latency budget for a mobile app calling a 3-service backend in one region.

  • Edge: terminate TLS at a regional edge near users; HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 with resumption.
  • Inside: pooled, warm connections between services, so internal calls pay only RTT + think.
  • Budget: 300 ms p99, split per segment and per hop, owned by named teams.
  • Measure: client-side segment spans in production, not only server spans.

Compare

Cold request Warm (reused connection) 0-RTT resumption
RTTs before the first response byte 3 + DNS 1 1, data in the first flight
Cost at 150 ms RTT, 40 ms think 520 ms 190 ms about 190 ms, plus TCP if not QUIC
Risk none stale connection to a dead peer replayable early data
How to get it default pool and keep-alive TLS 1.3 or QUIC session tickets

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
TCP handshake 1 RTT before any application byte spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 9293
TLS 1.3 full handshake 1 RTT TLS 1.2: 2 RTT spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 8446 §2
Cold call, 150 ms RTT 520 ms 30 ms DNS, 40 ms think derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Localhost cold vs reused, 120 ms handler 134 ms vs 131 ms total setup ≈ 3.5 ms locally measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Linux initial SYN retransmission 1 s why a lost SYN is a 1 s step default (as of Nov 2026): RFC 6298

Pitfalls

  • "Server time is what I should optimise"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the part you own and can profile.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: at real distances setup is three RTTs, so halving the handler buys 4 % at 150 ms RTT.
    ↳ Think instead: measure segments first, then fix the biggest one, usually with reuse.
  • "TTFB is server processing time"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: browser dev tools label that bar "waiting for server response".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it includes one RTT for the request and response to cross the network, and any queueing.
    ↳ Think instead: TTFB − RTT = think + queue.
  • Don't measure from your laptop and call it the user's latency.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: curl is right there and the numbers look precise.
    ↳ What goes wrong: your RTT, resolver and warm caches differ from your users'; you fix the wrong segment.
    ↳ Do instead: measure from where callers run, and collect client-side segment spans.
  • Not the same: latency vs throughput limits
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both make a download "slow".
    ↳ Difference: small responses are bounded by RTTs; large ones by bandwidth and the congestion window.
    ↳ Think instead: small payload: count RTTs; big payload: check throughput.
  • "curl's numbers are per-segment durations"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the variables are named like durations, time_connect and so on.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they're cumulative timestamps from the start, so each one includes all earlier segments.
    ↳ Think instead: subtract neighbours to get each segment.
  • Shelf life: the five segments and RTT counting are durable; HTTP/3 and curl's variable set move.

Connections

Path:TCP handshakewhere latency goespooling and keep-alivetimeouts
  • Builds on TLS 1.3 handshake and DNS resolution.
  • Owned elsewhere: latency, bandwidth, throughput owns the physics; tail latency owns percentiles.
  • Breaks when combined with a client that opens a new connection per request.
  • Bounded by queueing theory: past ~70 % utilisation, wait time grows faster than anything else.

notes.title: Connection Pooling & Keep-Alive — The Highest-Leverage Client Fix, Sized by Little's Law
notes.html:
References

RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1, §9 connection management · nginx: upstream keepalive · AWS: ALB idle timeout · Linux ip(7): ip_local_port_range

TL;DR

A reused connection skips DNS, the TCP handshake and the TLS handshake: two RTTs plus a lookup, and the handshake CPU, on every request. A pool keeps connections warm and hands them out. Three rules make it work:

  • Size by Little's Law: connections in use = request rate × time per request.
  • Idle timeout shorter than every peer's, so you close a quiet connection before they do.
  • Bound the pool, so a slow dependency queues callers instead of opening thousands of sockets.

Without pooling, a busy client also runs out of ephemeral ports: every closed connection sits in TIME_WAIT for 60 s.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:requestpool has an idle connection?yes: send now, no handshakesno, below max: dial (DNS + TCP + TLS)at max: wait (bounded)responseconnection back to the poolclosed by us after the idle timeout

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does reuse remove? DNS, TCP and TLS: 2 RTT + lookup and the handshake CPU, per request.
Pool size by Little's Law? L = λW: 2,000 rps × 40 ms = 80 connections in use.
Whose idle timeout must be shorter? The client's (the side that reuses), shorter than every server and LB on the path.
What runs out without a pool? Ephemeral ports: about 28,000 per destination, each held 60 s in TIME_WAIT.
The nginx default that kills upstream reuse? Before 1.29.7, proxy_http_version 1.0 and no keepalive in the upstream block.
Draw by hand: a pool a box of N connections (some busy, some idle), requests queuing at the door when all are busy, a dial arrow for new ones, and an idle-timeout clock that closes quiet ones before the server's clock does.

The idea

A service calls an internal API at 2,000 requests per second and opens a new connection each time. On a quiet day it's slow but works. At a traffic peak, calls start failing with EADDRNOTAVAIL: "cannot assign requested address". Each closed connection waits 60 s in TIME_WAIT, so the client holds 120,000 sockets to one destination, and Linux has about 28,000 ports to give.

With a pool, the same traffic needs about 80 connections, open for hours.

The trade: pooling removes handshakes and port churn from every request, and you pay with state to manage: stale connections the peer already closed, a size to choose, and timeouts that must line up across every hop.

How it works

Where reuse breaks: every idle timer on the path, and which one must fire first.

Rule Value Why
Pool size in use λ × W = 2,000 × 0.040 = 80 Little's Law; set max at 1.5–2× for bursts
Client idle timeout below the smallest idle timer downstream otherwise the peer closes it and your next write gets a reset
Each hop's idle timeout longer than the hop before it the side that reuses must give up first
Max connections bounded, with a wait timeout an unbounded pool turns a slow dependency into thousands of sockets
Max lifetime minutes, with jitter lets DNS and LB changes take effect; avoids synchronized reconnects 
without a pool: sockets in TIME_WAIT = rps × 60 s     ← 2,000 × 60 = 120,000 > 28,232 ports
ports per (src IP, dst IP, dst port) = 60999 − 32768 + 1 = 28,232
with a pool:    connections = rps × service time       ← 2,000 × 0.040 = 80

Evolution

Lineage:1996 HTTP/1.0, one request per connection1997 HTTP/1.1 persistent connections by default2015 HTTP/2: one connection, many streams2022 HTTP/3 connection migration2026 nginx 1.29.7 makes upstream HTTP/1.1 keep-alive the default
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: nginx 1.29.7 turned on upstream keep-alive by default, ending its best-known pooling trap; HTTP/2 client pools hold few connections with many streams each.
  • What won't change: a handshake costs round trips, and the side that reuses must close first.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15 http.client against a local HTTPS server with a 2 ms handler, 200 requests each way):

python3 pool.py
# new connection each time: 4.23 ms/request · reused: 2.80 ms/request · saved 34%
# new connection each time: 3.90 ms/request · reused: 2.77 ms/request · saved 29%   ← second run
# RTT here is ~0.05 ms, so the saving is handshake CPU alone; at 20 ms RTT add 40 ms per request

The nginx upstream block, with the defaults that bite on versions before 1.29.7:

upstream api {
    server 10.0.1.10:8080;
    keepalive 64;                 # idle connections kept per worker; no default before 1.29.7
    keepalive_timeout 60s;
}
location / {
    proxy_pass http://api;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;       # default 1.0 before 1.29.7: a new upstream connection per request
    proxy_set_header Connection "";   # don't forward the client's "Connection: close"
}

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): ports held in TIME_WAIT when every request opens and closes its own connection.

for rps in (200, 470, 2000):
    print(rps, rps * 60, "EXHAUSTED" if rps * 60 > 28_232 else "ok")
print("pooled:", 2000 * 0.040)
# look for: the 2,000 rps row
# naive belief predicts: closing connections promptly frees resources

Run: 200 rps holds 12,000 sockets (fine), 470 rps holds 28,200 (at the edge), 2,000 rps needs 120,000 against 28,232 ports, so it's exhausted. Pooled, the same 2,000 rps uses 80 connections.

Measure it

  • See it: ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l on the client; ss -tn dst <ip> to count live connections per destination; curl -w '%{num_connects}' across two URLs shows reuse.
  • In production: new connections per second vs requests per second (the reuse ratio), pool wait time and pool-exhausted errors, TCP resets after idle periods, EADDRNOTAVAIL errors.
  • Bounded by: stale-connection resets → keep-alives and idle timeouts; ports → sockets and the ephemeral range.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Reusing connections removes DNS, TCP and TLS from every request: two RTTs plus handshake CPU. I size the pool with Little's Law, rate times latency, and cap it with a wait timeout. I set the client's idle timeout below every server and LB idle timeout so we close first, and add a max lifetime so DNS changes take effect. Without a pool, TIME_WAIT eats the ephemeral ports at a few hundred rps per destination.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a pooled connection sometimes fail on its first request after a quiet period? The server or LB closed it at its idle timeout and sent a FIN, but the client didn't read it before reusing the connection. The client writes, the peer answers with a reset, and the request fails, possibly after the server saw nothing. Fix: client idle timeout below the peer's, and retry once on a connection reset before any response byte (safe, see retries).

Q · Trade-off — Many HTTP/1.1 connections or a few HTTP/2 connections? HTTP/1.1 needs one connection per in-flight request, so pools are large but spread naturally across backends. HTTP/2 multiplexes, so a few connections carry everything: fewer handshakes and sockets, but load pins to the few backends those connections reach, and one lost packet stalls all streams on TCP. HTTP/2 to a balancer that spreads streams; HTTP/1.1 pools or HTTP/2 with several connections to bare backends.

Q · Failure — After a dependency slows from 40 ms to 2 s, the caller runs out of memory. Why? Little's Law: in-flight work grew 50× (λ × W). An unbounded pool opened 50× the connections, with buffers and threads behind each. Fix: a bounded pool with a short acquire timeout, so callers fail fast instead of piling up, plus a breaker (breakers and bulkheads).

Q · Design — Connection management for a service calling five internal APIs and one external one.

  • Per destination: a separate bounded pool, sized by λ × W at peak with 1.5× headroom.
  • Timers: client idle 50 s under a 60 s ALB; max lifetime 5 minutes with jitter.
  • External API: egress through a proxy that keeps a warm pool to the vendor, so pods don't each pay the long-RTT handshake.
  • Watch: reuse ratio, pool wait p99 and resets per minute.

Compare

New connection per request HTTP/1.1 pool HTTP/2 (few connections)
Handshakes every request once per connection once per connection
Connections at 2,000 rps × 40 ms 120,000 in TIME_WAIT ~80 a handful
Spread across backends per request per connection, many per connection, few: watch pinning
Failure blast radius one request one request every stream on that connection

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Ephemeral ports, Linux default 32768–60999 (28,232) per (src IP, dst IP, dst port) default (as of Nov 2026): Linux ip(7)
TIME_WAIT on Linux 60 s held by the side that closes first default (as of Nov 2026): Linux kernel TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN
ALB idle timeout 60 s the common downstream bound default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB attributes
Localhost saving from reuse, 2 ms handler 29–34 % handshake CPU only measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Pool in use, 2,000 rps × 40 ms 80 Little's Law derived; model run 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Closing connections after each request is tidier"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no state to manage and no stale connections to worry about.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: every request pays the handshakes, and TIME_WAIT exhausts ports at a few hundred rps per destination.
    ↳ Think instead: pool, and manage the state with idle and lifetime limits.
  • Don't let the client's idle timeout exceed the server's.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: longer idle time means more reuse.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the server closes first, and the client's next write on that connection gets a reset.
    ↳ Do instead: client idle < smallest peer idle on the path, by a margin of seconds.
  • "A bigger pool is always safer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no request ever waits for a connection.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: when a dependency slows, an unbounded pool opens connections in proportion, moving the overload into memory, threads and the dependency itself.
    ↳ Think instead: bound it at λW × headroom and fail fast when full.
  • Not the same: HTTP keep-alive vs TCP keepalive
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same word, both about idle connections.
    ↳ Difference: HTTP keep-alive means reusing a connection for more requests; TCP keepalive sends probes to detect a dead peer, by default after 2 hours.
    ↳ Think instead: reuse vs liveness: two different settings.
  • Don't keep connections forever.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: maximum reuse, no reconnect cost.
    ↳ What goes wrong: DNS changes, new backends and LB moves are never seen; old backends keep all the load.
    ↳ Do instead: a max lifetime of minutes, with jitter.
  • Shelf life: Little's Law and the close-first rule are durable; server defaults (nginx 1.29.7) and LB timeouts move.

Connections

Path:where latency goespooling and keep-alivetimeoutsqueueing theory
  • Builds on connection teardown (TIME_WAIT) and HTTP/1.0 vs 1.1.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC load balancing owns HTTP/2 pinning.
  • Breaks when combined with a client idle timeout longer than a peer's.
  • Bounded by the ephemeral port range.

notes.title: Timeout Hierarchy — Four Timers, and Why Inner Must Be Shorter Than Outer
notes.html:
References

Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter · gRPC: Deadlines · nginx: proxy_read_timeout · Envoy: Timeouts FAQ

TL;DR

"The timeout" is four different timers, and they measure different things:

  • Connect: how long to wait for the handshake; it bounds one or two RTTs.
  • Read (or write): the longest gap between bytes, not the total duration.
  • Total (deadline): the whole call, retries included.
  • Idle: how long an unused connection may live.

Across a chain of services they must nest: each inner call's total, times its attempts, must fit inside the outer one. If it doesn't, the outer hop gives up first, blames the wrong component, and the inner work keeps running for nobody. Propagating one deadline through the chain enforces the nesting automatically.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:edge deadline 10 sservice A gets 9.5 s leftcalls B with 4 s × 2 attemptsB calls the database with 1.5 seach hop passes the remaining budget downany hop out of budget fails fast instead of starting work

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four timers? Connect, read/write (gap between bytes), total (deadline), idle.
What does a read timeout measure? The gap between bytes; a slow steady stream never trips it.
The nesting rule? attempts × (inner total + backoff) < outer total.
What happens if an inner timeout exceeds the outer? The outer hop gives up first; the inner work runs on, wasted.
Which timer must a streaming response leave unset? Total; keep read bounded so a stalled stream is caught.
Draw by hand: nested deadlines three stacked bars (edge 10 s, service 4 s × 2 attempts, database 1.5 s), each strictly inside the one above, with an arrow labelled "remaining budget" passed down.

The idea

An API gateway gives up after 10 s and returns 504. Behind it, a service calls a slow search backend with a 30 s timeout. When search degrades, the gateway returns 504 at 10 s, and the service keeps waiting for another 18 s on every one of those calls. Its worker pool fills with work no one will read, and healthy requests start queuing behind it. The incident report blames the gateway, which was the only component that behaved correctly.

The trade: nested, propagated deadlines make every hop give up together and stop wasted work early, and you pay by having to budget time across teams, and by failing calls that might have succeeded given a little longer.

How it works

The nesting, hop by hop.

Timer Measures Size it from Wrong when
connect the handshake 2–3 × RTT, plus SYN retry: 1–2 s in-region it's 30 s: a dead host holds a worker that long
read / write the gap between bytes the longest legitimate pause it's used as a total limit
total / deadline the whole call, retries included caller's remaining budget it's longer than the caller's
idle an unused connection below the peer's idle timer it's above the peer's (pooling) 
nesting:        attempts × (T_inner + backoff) < T_outer      ← 2 × (4 + 0.5) = 9 < 9.5 ✓
wasted work:    f × λ × (T_inner − T_outer) worker-seconds/s   ← 10 % × 50 rps × (28 − 10) = 90

90 worker-seconds per second means 90 workers permanently busy on abandoned calls.

Evolution

Lineage:1980s socket SO_RCVTIMEO per read2015 gRPC deadlines propagated across calls2017 Envoy per-route and per-try timeouts2019 Amazon Builders' Library publishes the nesting rule2020s context and AbortSignal deadlines in Go, .NET and the web platform
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: deadline propagation is built into gRPC, Go context and AbortSignal.timeout(); meshes enforce per-try timeouts.
  • What won't change: a read timeout is a gap timer; total time needs its own bound.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (Python 3.15 sockets): a client with a 1 s timeout reads from a server that sends one byte at a fixed interval.

python3 drip.py
# byte every 0.5 s: finished after 4.0 s, 8 bytes, read timeout never fired
# byte every 2.0 s: read timeout after 1.0 s, 1 bytes
# the 1 s timeout bounded each GAP, never the 4 s total: a slow drip runs as long as it likes

An Envoy route with the timers that bite:

route:
  timeout: 9s                    # total, including retries. Default 15 s: longer than most edge budgets
  retry_policy:
    num_retries: 1
    per_try_timeout: 4s          # default: unset, so each try may use the whole 9 s
  idle_timeout: 50s              # stream idle; default 5 min on the connection manager
# nginx's proxy_read_timeout default is 60 s BETWEEN READS: a backend that drips a byte every 59 s holds forever

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): worker time spent on calls the caller already abandoned.

f, lam, slow, outer = 0.10, 50, 28, 10     # 10 % of calls take 28 s; caller gives up at 10 s
print(f * lam * (slow - outer))             # inner timeout 30 s
print(0)                                    # inner timeout 8 s: work stops before the caller leaves
# look for: worker-seconds per second
# naive belief predicts: a longer inner timeout is safer because fewer calls fail

Run: 90 worker-seconds per second wasted with the 30 s inner timeout, 0 with 8 s. A pool of 64 workers is saturated by abandoned work alone.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w '%{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}' against each hop; compare where each call ends against each hop's configured timers.
  • In production: timeouts by hop and by timer type (connect vs read vs total), work still running after its caller returned (log the remaining deadline at start), 504s at the edge next to the backend's own latency.
  • Bounded by: retry multiplication → retries; connection idle → keep-alives and idle timeouts.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: There are four timers: connect, read or write between bytes, total, and idle. The read timeout doesn't bound duration, so every call needs a total. Across a chain they must nest: attempts times inner total, plus backoff, must fit inside the outer. Best is propagating one deadline, as gRPC does, so each hop knows the remaining budget and refuses to start work it can't finish.

Q · Mechanism — How does deadline propagation differ from static timeouts? A static timeout is fixed per hop and ignores time already spent. A propagated deadline is an absolute time sent with the request (gRPC's grpc-timeout header, recomputed per hop). Each hop sets its local timeout to the remaining budget minus a margin, and if the remaining budget is already too small, it fails at once instead of doing doomed work.

Q · Trade-off — Tight or generous timeouts? Tight timeouts free workers fast and keep failures cheap, but cut off legitimately slow calls and, with retries, add load. Generous timeouts let slow calls finish but hold resources during a slowdown and invert the nesting. Set total from the caller's budget and p99.9, connect from RTT, and keep retries inside the budget.

Q · Failure — The edge reports 504s, but the backend shows almost no errors. Why? The backend's timeouts are longer than the edge's. It eventually succeeds, at 25 s, long after the edge returned 504 at 10 s, so its own metrics look healthy. The sign is backend latency above the edge timeout. Fix the nesting, propagate the deadline, and have the backend stop when the client goes away.

Q · Design — A timeout policy for a chain: edge → API → 3 internal services → database.

  • Edge: a 10 s total; deadline sent downstream.
  • Each hop: total = remaining budget − 0.5 s margin; at most one retry, only if budget remains.
  • Connect: 1 s everywhere in-region.
  • Streams: no total, a read gap timeout of 30 s, plus heartbeats.
  • Watch: timeouts per hop and timer type, and work running past its deadline.

Compare

Static per-hop timeouts Propagated deadline
Knows time already spent no yes
Nesting by careful configuration automatic
Doomed work starts anyway refused at the hop
Needs config per hop a header and library support (gRPC, context)

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
nginx proxy_read_timeout 60 s between reads a gap timer default (as of Nov 2026): nginx proxy module
Envoy route timeout 15 s total, including retries default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy timeouts FAQ
Wasted work, 10 % slow, 50 rps, 18 s over 90 worker-seconds/s inner 30 s vs outer 10 s derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Slow drip under a 1 s read timeout 4.0 s, never fired a byte every 0.5 s measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "A read timeout of 5 s means calls end within 5 s"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: most libraries call it just "timeout".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it bounds the gap between bytes; a slow drip of a byte every 4 s runs forever.
    ↳ Think instead: always set a total as well, except on streams.
  • "Longer inner timeouts mean fewer failures"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: calls that would have succeeded at 25 s now do.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: if the caller left at 10 s, the success goes to nobody, and the worker time is lost.
    ↳ Think instead: inner < outer, always; propagate the deadline.
  • Don't leave connect timeouts at library defaults.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: connects are usually fast, so nobody notices.
    ↳ What goes wrong: defaults of 30–120 s (or the kernel's SYN retries) hold a worker that long for a dead host.
    ↳ Do instead: 1–2 s in-region, derived from RTT and one SYN retry.
  • Not the same: timeout vs deadline
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both stop a call that takes too long.
    ↳ Difference: a timeout is a duration per hop; a deadline is an absolute time shared by the whole chain.
    ↳ Think instead: durations don't compose; deadlines do.
  • "A timeout means the server didn't do the work"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the caller got no answer.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the server may have completed it after the caller left; retrying can duplicate the effect.
    ↳ Think instead: a timeout is "unknown", so retries need idempotency (idempotency).
  • Shelf life: the four timers and the nesting rule are durable; proxy defaults move.

Connections

Path:poolingtimeout hierarchyretriesbreakers
  • Builds on timeouts, retries and backoff: the HTTP contract and backoff strategies.
  • Owned elsewhere: keep-alives and idle timeouts owns idle timers.
  • Breaks when combined with retries that don't fit inside the caller's budget.
  • Bounded by queueing theory: abandoned work is load.

notes.title: Retries Done Right — Gate on Safety, Budget in Successes, Retry at One Layer
notes.html:
References

Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter · Google SRE book: Handling overload, client-side throttling · RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent methods · Envoy: Retry budgets

TL;DR

A retry turns a transient failure into a success, and a sustained failure into extra load. Three rules keep it on the right side:

  • Gate: retry only what's safe. Connection failures before any byte was sent are always safe. Idempotent methods are safe. A timeout on a POST is safe only with an idempotency key.
  • Budget: cap retries as a fraction of successful requests (around 10 %), so retries shrink as failures grow instead of multiplying them.
  • One layer: retry at one hop only. Three hops each trying 3 times send 27 requests to the deepest service for one user request.

Back off with jitter so retries don't arrive in synchronized waves.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:call failssafe to repeat? (connection error, idempotent, or keyed)budget left? (retries < 10 % of recent successes)deadline left?wait with jittered backoffretry, preferably on another hostotherwise return the error

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which failures are always safe to retry? Connection-level ones before any request byte reached the app.
What makes a POST retryable? An idempotency key the server deduplicates on.
What is a retry budget? Retries capped at a fraction (~10 %) of successful requests.
3 hops × 3 attempts reaches the bottom how many times? 3³ = 27.
Why is a timeout the riskiest thing to retry? The work may have completed; a retry can duplicate it.
Draw by hand: retry amplification three hops stacked, each fanning to 3 arrows, ending in 27 arrows at the database; beside it the same chain with retries only at the top: 3 arrows.

The idea

A database slows down for a minute. The service in front of it retries 3 times; so does the API above that; so does the mobile SDK above that. The database, already struggling, now gets up to 27 requests for every user action, and the request rate on its dashboard triples while users get nothing. It never recovers on its own, because the retries are the load.

The trade: retries hide transient faults from users almost for free, and you pay with load multiplication during exactly the outages where load hurts most, unless retries are gated, budgeted and confined to one layer.

How it works

Where to retry, and where not.

Failure Retry? Why
connect refused, reset before sending yes the request never reached the app
503 with Retry-After, 429 yes, after the delay the server asked you to come back
timeout on GET, PUT, DELETE yes, within budget idempotent by definition (RFC 9110)
timeout on POST only with an idempotency key the effect may already have happened
400, 401, 403, 404, 422 no the same request will fail the same way 
amplification across n hops, k attempts each      = kⁿ            ← 3³ = 27
expected load per hop at failure rate p, k tries  = 1 + p + … + p^(k−1)   ← p = 0.9: 2.71×; 3 hops: 19.9×
with a 10 % budget per hop                        ≤ 1.1ⁿ          ← 3 hops: 1.33×, whatever p is

Evolution

Lineage:1970s Ethernet exponential backoff2015 AWS "exponential backoff and jitter"2016 Google SRE book: client-side throttling2017 Envoy retry budgets2019 Amazon Builders' Library: retry at one layer2022 RFC 9110 restates idempotent methods
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: meshes and gRPC (retryPolicy, retryThrottling) ship budgets as config; the IETF idempotency-key header draft is widely implemented by APIs.
  • What won't change: a retry is new load, and a timeout can't tell you whether work happened.

On the wire

A gRPC service config with retries gated and throttled, and the defaults that bite:

{
  "methodConfig": [{
    "name": [{ "service": "orders.Orders", "method": "Get" }],
    "retryPolicy": {
      "maxAttempts": 3,
      "initialBackoff": "0.1s", "maxBackoff": "1s", "backoffMultiplier": 2,
      "retryableStatusCodes": ["UNAVAILABLE"]
    }
  }],
  "retryThrottling": { "maxTokens": 10, "tokenRatio": 0.1 }
}

retryThrottling is the budget: each failure spends a token, each success earns back 0.1, and retries stop while tokens are below half. The default that bites: SDKs and HTTP clients often retry on their own (AWS SDKs 3 attempts by default, many browsers resend idempotent requests on reset), so a "no retries" service can still be retried twice upstream.

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): load reaching the deepest service, per user request.

def per_hop(p, k): return sum(p**i for i in range(k))
for p in (0.1, 0.5, 0.9):
    print(p, round(per_hop(p, 3), 2), round(per_hop(p, 3) ** 3, 1), round(1.1 ** 3, 2))
# look for: p = 0.9, three hops
# naive belief predicts: retries only matter for the few requests that fail

Run: at 10 % failure, 1.11× per hop and 1.4× through three hops; at 50 %, 5.4×; at 90 %, 19.9×. With a 10 % retry budget at each hop the worst case is 1.33×, whatever the failure rate. Worst case without budgets: 3³ = 27×.

Measure it

  • See it: request rate vs success rate on one graph during an incident: rising requests with falling successes is retry load.
  • In production: retries as a share of requests per caller and per hop, budget-exhausted counts, attempts per user request (from trace span counts).
  • Bounded by: the caller's deadline → timeouts; duplicate effects → idempotency.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I retry only what's safe: connection failures, idempotent methods, or POSTs with an idempotency key. I cap retries with a budget of about 10 % of successes so they shrink in an outage, back off with jitter, keep attempts inside the deadline, and retry at one layer only, because 3 attempts at 3 hops means 27 requests at the bottom.

Q · Mechanism — Why denominate the budget in successes rather than requests? A budget of "10 % of requests" grows with the retries themselves, so in an outage it still adds load. "10 % of successes" shrinks as successes fall: when nothing succeeds, almost no retries are allowed. It's a feedback loop that turns retries off automatically when they can't help.

Q · Trade-off — Retry at the edge or deep in the stack? At the edge, one retry covers the whole chain and the deep services see at most one extra request. Deep in the stack, retries are faster and can switch hosts cheaply, but every layer that also retries multiplies. Retry at one layer, usually the one closest to the failure that can pick another host, and make every other layer pass errors through.

Q · Failure — During an outage, request rate to the database tripled while traffic was flat. What happened? Nested retries: each hop retried its own failed calls, so the database saw kⁿ attempts per user request. The signature is requests up, successes down, users flat. Stop it by shedding at the database, turning off inner retries, and adding budgets so it can't recur.

Q · Design — A retry policy for a payment flow across gateway → payments service → card processor.

  • Gateway: retries connection errors only.
  • Payments service: the one retrying layer, toward the processor, with an idempotency key per payment and a 10 % budget.
  • Timeouts: attempts × (per-try + backoff) inside the caller's deadline.
  • Unknown outcome: on timeout, query the processor by key before any new attempt.
  • Watch: retry share, budget exhaustion and duplicate-key hits.

Compare

No retries Retries at every hop One layer, budgeted
Transient fault seen by user yes no no
Worst-case load at the bottom, 3 hops 1× 27× 1.33×
Behaviour in a long outage fails fast amplifies, delays recovery backs off automatically
Duplicate effects none likely without keys only if unkeyed

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Retry budget, gRPC throttling a success earns 0.1 token ≈ 10 % of successes; Envoy's own budget defaults to 20 % of active requests spec (as of Nov 2026): gRPC gRFC A6, Envoy retry budget docs
Amplification, 3 hops × 3 attempts 27× kⁿ derived
Expected load through 3 hops at 90 % failure 19.9× geometric series per hop derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Same, with a 10 % budget per hop 1.33× 1.1³ derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
AWS SDK default attempts 3 "standard" retry mode default (as of Nov 2026): AWS SDK retry behavior docs

Pitfalls

  • "Retries only touch the requests that fail"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: in normal times, retry traffic is a rounding error.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in an outage most requests fail, so retries multiply total load just when capacity is lowest.
    ↳ Think instead: budget in successes, so retries fade as failures grow.
  • Don't retry at every layer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each team adds retries to make its own service look reliable.
    ↳ What goes wrong: attempts multiply per hop; 3 at 3 hops is 27 at the bottom.
    ↳ Do instead: one retrying layer; everyone else passes errors up.
  • "A timeout means it failed, so retry"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the caller saw an error.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the server may have finished the work after the caller left; a retry charges the card twice.
    ↳ Think instead: timeout = unknown; retry only with an idempotency key.
  • Not the same: backoff vs jitter
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "wait before retrying".
    ↳ Difference: backoff spreads attempts out in time per client; jitter spreads them across clients, so they don't arrive together.
    ↳ Think instead: backoff for the client, jitter for the fleet.
  • "No retries in our code means no retries"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nobody wrote a retry loop.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: SDKs, HTTP clients, meshes and browsers retry by default, often 2–3 times.
    ↳ Think instead: inventory every layer's defaults and turn off the ones you don't want.
  • Shelf life: gate, budget and one layer are durable; SDK and mesh defaults move.

Connections

Path:timeoutsretriesbreakers and sheddingcascading failures
  • Builds on safe and idempotent methods and backoff and jitter.
  • Owned elsewhere: idempotency keys owns the key contract.
  • Breaks when combined with retries at several hops, or retried timeouts on unkeyed writes.
  • Bounded by the caller's deadline: attempts must fit inside it.

notes.title: Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads & Load Shedding — Failing Fast to Protect Caller, Peers and Callee
notes.html:
References

Martin Fowler: Circuit Breaker · Envoy: Circuit breaking · Amazon Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload · Google SRE book: Handling overload

TL;DR

Three patterns, each protecting a different party:

  • Circuit breaker protects the caller. After enough failures it opens and fails calls instantly, then lets one trial call through (half-open) to test recovery.
  • Bulkhead protects the caller's other work. Each dependency gets its own bounded pool, so one slow dependency can't take every thread.
  • Load shedding protects the callee. Past capacity it rejects cheaply instead of queuing.

Queuing past capacity makes every request late: goodput falls toward zero while the server stays 100 % busy. Rejecting some keeps the rest on time.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:dependency slowsbulkhead caps its in-flight calls at 20calls beyond that fail fasterrors pass the threshold, breaker opensfallback servedafter 30 s one trial callsuccess closes the breaker

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three breaker states? Closed (passing), open (failing fast), half-open (trial calls).
Who does each pattern protect? Breaker: the caller. Bulkhead: the caller's other work. Shedding: the callee.
What does Envoy call circuit breaking? Concurrency limits: max connections, pending and active requests, retries. No timed states.
Why shed rather than queue? Past capacity, queued work finishes after clients time out: zero goodput.
What does a breaker need to be useful? A fallback; otherwise it only moves the error closer to the user.
Draw by hand: three states three circles: closed → (failure rate over threshold) → open → (timer) → half-open → (trial succeeds) → closed, and (trial fails) → open.

The idea

A checkout service calls recommendations, inventory and payments from one 200-thread pool. Recommendations slows to 30 s per call. Within a minute all 200 threads are waiting on it, and checkout, which doesn't even need recommendations to finish, stops responding. A bulkhead of 20 threads for recommendations would have cost 20 threads, and a breaker would have stopped calling it at all.

Meanwhile, recommendations is receiving more traffic than it can serve and queuing all of it. Every request it finishes is already past its caller's timeout, so it does 100 % work for 0 % useful output.

The trade: failing fast keeps the healthy parts of a system healthy and the overloaded part productive, and you pay by deliberately failing some requests that might have succeeded, and by needing fallbacks and tuned thresholds.

How it works

The breaker's states.

Pattern Protects Mechanism Trigger Needs
circuit breaker the caller stop calling, fail instantly error or slow-call rate over a window a fallback
bulkhead the caller's other work a bounded pool per dependency the pool is full sizing by λ × W
load shedding the callee reject before doing work queue or concurrency past a limit rejection far cheaper than service
Envoy "circuit breaker" the upstream caps connections, pending, requests, retries a cap reached per-cluster limits 
bulkhead size = λ × W at normal latency × headroom   ← 100 rps × 0.1 s × 2 = 20 threads
during a slowdown, the bulkhead caps damage at 20 threads, not λ × W_slow = 100 × 30 = 3,000

Evolution

Lineage:2007 Nygard, Release It!: breaker and bulkhead2012 Netflix Hystrix2016 Google SRE book: overload and client throttling2017 Envoy circuit-breaking thresholds2018 Hystrix to maintenance; resilience4j2019 adaptive concurrency limits (Netflix concurrency-limits, Envoy filter)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: adaptive concurrency limits replace fixed thresholds; meshes apply breakers and outlier ejection per host without code.
  • What won't change: past capacity, rejecting serves more users than queuing.

On the wire

An Envoy cluster with concurrency limits and outlier ejection, with the defaults that bite:

clusters:
- name: recommendations
  circuit_breakers:
    thresholds:
    - max_connections: 100         # default 1024
      max_pending_requests: 20     # default 1024: a queue that deep is pure latency
      max_requests: 50             # default 1024 in-flight; this IS the bulkhead
      max_retries: 3               # default 3 concurrent retries cluster-wide
  outlier_detection:
    consecutive_5xx: 5             # eject a host after 5 straight 5xx
    base_ejection_time: 30s
# Envoy has no open/half-open timer per route; ejection per host plays that role

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): a server with capacity 100 rps, clients that give up after 1 s, 60 s of load.

def run(offered, shed, cap=100, timeout=1.0, limit=50):
    # Poisson arrivals; FIFO service at 10 ms each; with shed=True, reject when 50 are queued
    # count only responses that finish within the client's 1 s timeout (goodput)
    ...
for off in (80, 120, 200): print(off, run(off, False), run(off, True))
# look for: goodput at 120 and 200 rps
# naive belief predicts: queueing everything serves at least as many as rejecting some

Run: at 80 rps, 80 good responses/s either way (78 when shedding). At 120 rps, queuing everything gives 10/s good responses, while shedding past 50 queued gives 101/s. At 200 rps it's 4/s vs 101/s. The queuing server is 100 % busy the whole time.

Measure it

  • See it: breaker state per dependency on a dashboard; curl the admin endpoint (/clusters in Envoy) for rq_pending_overflow and cx_open counters.
  • In production: goodput (successes within deadline) vs throughput, rejections by reason, breaker opens per hour, bulkhead saturation per dependency, fallback rate.
  • Bounded by: threshold tuning against real latency → queueing theory; recovery storms → cascading failures.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Three patterns, three beneficiaries. A breaker protects the caller: stop calling a failing dependency, serve a fallback, probe with half-open. A bulkhead protects the caller's other work: a bounded pool per dependency. Shedding protects the callee: reject cheaply past capacity, because queuing past capacity drives goodput to zero. In a mesh, Envoy implements the first two as concurrency limits and outlier ejection.

Q · Mechanism — Why does goodput collapse when a server queues everything? Past capacity, the queue grows without limit, and every request waits behind it. Once the wait exceeds the client timeout, the server spends all its capacity on responses no one will read. Throughput stays at 100 %; goodput falls toward zero. Shedding keeps the queue short, so the requests it accepts finish in time.

Q · Trade-off — Fixed thresholds or adaptive concurrency limits? Fixed thresholds are simple and predictable but wrong whenever latency or capacity changes, which is exactly during incidents. Adaptive limits (gradient or AIMD, like TCP congestion control) measure latency and shrink the limit as it rises. Adaptive at the server for shedding; fixed bulkheads per dependency at the client, sized from Little's Law.

Q · Failure — The breaker opened, the dependency recovered, and then it went down again immediately. Why? On close, every caller resumed at full rate at the same moment, along with queued retries and cold caches. The recovering service got a step load it couldn't absorb. Fix: half-open with a few trial calls, then ramp traffic gradually, with jittered open timers so callers don't close together.

Q · Design — Protecting a checkout flow with three dependencies, one optional.

  • Bulkheads: separate pools for recommendations (20), inventory (40), payments (40), sized by λ × W.
  • Breakers: on recommendations with an empty-list fallback; on inventory with a cached-stock fallback; none on payments, which fails the checkout honestly.
  • Shedding: each dependency sheds by priority, checkout traffic before browse traffic.
  • Watch: goodput, breaker state and fallback rate.

Compare

Circuit breaker Bulkhead Load shedding
Lives in the caller the caller the callee
Protects the caller's latency the caller's other dependencies the callee's goodput
Acts on error and slow-call rate concurrency per dependency queue depth or concurrency
User sees fallback fast error for one feature fast 503 or 429

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Breaker states 3 closed, open, half-open spec (as of Nov 2026): Fowler, Circuit Breaker
Envoy thresholds 1024 connections, pending, requests; 3 retries per cluster default (as of Nov 2026): Envoy circuit breaking
Goodput at 200 rps offered, capacity 100 4/s queuing vs 101/s shedding 1 s client timeout derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Bulkhead, 100 rps × 0.1 s × 2 20 vs 3,000 threads at 30 s latency derived

Pitfalls

  • "Queuing is kinder than rejecting"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every request eventually gets an answer.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: past capacity the answers arrive after clients have given up, so the server works at 100 % for nobody.
    ↳ Think instead: bound the queue at what finishes within the timeout, and reject the rest.
  • Don't add a breaker without a fallback.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: failing fast sounds good on its own.
    ↳ What goes wrong: users see the same error, sooner; nothing is protected except the caller's threads.
    ↳ Do instead: a degraded answer (cache, default, partial page) or an honest fast error with a reason.
  • "One shared thread pool is more efficient"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no idle capacity sits reserved for one dependency.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the slowest dependency absorbs every thread (Little's Law), taking down unrelated features.
    ↳ Think instead: bulkhead per dependency, sized from rate × latency.
  • Not the same: Envoy circuit breaking vs a classic breaker
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same name in the docs.
    ↳ Difference: Envoy caps concurrency and has no open/half-open timer; a classic breaker tracks error rate and stops calling for a period.
    ↳ Think instead: Envoy's is a bulkhead; outlier ejection is its per-host breaker.
  • Don't make rejection expensive.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: logging, auth and parsing run before the shed check.
    ↳ What goes wrong: rejecting costs nearly as much as serving, so shedding saves nothing under overload.
    ↳ Do instead: shed first, at the edge of the process, before any real work.
  • Shelf life: the three patterns are durable; library names and adaptive algorithms move.

Connections

Path:retriesbreakers, bulkheads, sheddingdegradation and backpressurecascading failures
  • Builds on queueing theory: Little's Law sizes the bulkhead.
  • Owned elsewhere: outlier detection owns per-host ejection; rate limiting owns per-client quotas.
  • Breaks when combined with unbudgeted retries, which refill what shedding removed.
  • Bounded by fallback quality: a breaker is only as good as what it serves instead.

notes.title: Queueing Theory in One Page — Little's Law and the ρ/(1−ρ) Curve
notes.html:
References

Little, "A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW" (1961) · Google SRE book: Handling overload · Harchol-Balter: Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems, ch. 6 · Marc Brooker: Latency sneaks up on you

TL;DR

Two formulas cover most capacity and latency arguments:

  • Little's Law: L = λW. Work in the system = arrival rate × time each item spends there. It holds for any stable system, with no assumptions about distributions.
  • The utilisation curve: in a simple queue, waiting time grows as ρ / (1 − ρ). That's 1× at 50 % busy, 2.3× at 70 %, 9× at 90 % and 19× at 95 %.

The tail grows with the same factor, so p99 at 90 % utilisation is 5× p99 at 50 %. Latency-sensitive services run at 70–80 % at peak, because every point above that costs more latency than the one before.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:arrivals at rate λqueueserver busy fraction ρ = λ / μwait ∝ ρ / (1 − ρ)in-flight L = λWpast ρ ≈ 0.8 the curve turns vertical

Recall

Prompt Answer
Little's Law? L = λW: 500 rps × 40 ms = 20 in flight.
Wait factor at 50 %, 90 %, 99 % busy? 1, 9, 99 (ρ / (1 − ρ)).
Why does variability matter? More variable arrivals or service times multiply the queue at the same utilisation.

The idea

A team sees CPU at 60 % with p99 at 150 ms, and plans capacity linearly: 90 % CPU should give "about 1.5× the latency". At 90 %, p99 is 460 ms, 3× higher, and at 95 % it's 920 ms. The curve isn't linear. Each step toward 100 % costs more than the last, because a queue needs idle time to drain the bursts that random arrivals always bring.

The trade: running hotter saves servers, and you pay with latency that grows as 1 / (1 − ρ), so the last 20 % of utilisation costs more latency than the first 80 %.

How it works

An M/M/1 queue (random arrivals, random service, 10 ms mean service time). Time in system is exponential with rate μ − λ, so percentiles follow directly.

Utilisation ρ ρ / (1 − ρ) p50 p99
0.50 1.0 14 ms 92 ms
0.70 2.3 23 ms 154 ms
0.80 4.0 35 ms 230 ms
0.90 9.0 69 ms 461 ms
0.95 19.0 139 ms 921 ms 
ρ = λ / μ                       ← 90 rps into a server that does 100 rps: ρ = 0.9
time in system ~ Exp(μ − λ)     ← p = −ln(1 − q) / (μ − λ): p99 = ln(100) / 10 s⁻¹ = 461 ms
L = λW                          ← 90 rps × 0.1 s mean = 9 requests in the system

Computed with Python 3.15 on 24 Nov 2026. Real servers aren't M/M/1 (batching, multiple workers, GC), but the shape holds: flat, then a knee, then near-vertical.

Evolution

Lineage:1909 Erlang's telephone queues1953 Kendall notation (M/M/1)1961 Little's Law proof1980s Kingman's formula for variable service2016 Google SRE book applies it to overload
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: autoscalers and adaptive concurrency limits target utilisation and latency directly instead of fixed thresholds.
  • What won't change: L = λW, and a queue needs slack to absorb bursts.

On the wire

Little's Law applied to a live service, and the default that bites:

# from metrics: 500 rps, mean latency 40 ms
python3 -c "print(500 * 0.040)"      # 20.0   ← requests in flight on average
# the default that bites: autoscalers default to ~70-80 % CPU targets, but CPU lags queueing;
# a service blocked on I/O can be at 40 % CPU and still have a full worker pool

Measure it

  • See it: in-flight requests (or queue depth) next to rate × mean latency: if they disagree, a hidden queue exists somewhere.
  • In production: utilisation per bottleneck resource (worker pool, connections, CPU), queue depth and time spent queued, p99 against utilisation on one chart to find the knee.
  • Bounded by: variability → tail latency; sizing → capacity planning.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Little's Law, L = λW, gives concurrency from rate and latency and holds for any stable system. Waiting time grows as ρ / (1 − ρ), so latency is flat until about 70 %, then climbs steeply: 9× at 90 %. The tail climbs with it. So I plan latency-sensitive services for 70–80 % peak utilisation of the bottleneck resource, which is often a pool, not CPU.

Q · Mechanism — Why do queues form below 100 % utilisation? Arrivals are bursty: at 80 % average, some seconds bring 120 % of capacity and others 40 %. A burst builds a queue that drains only during idle time, and at high utilisation there's little idle time, so queues from one burst are still there when the next arrives. ρ / (1 − ρ) is that effect averaged out.

Q · Trade-off — Run hot to save cost, or cool for latency? Hot saves servers, but past the knee each extra point of utilisation costs disproportionate latency, and a small traffic spike pushes you to 100 % where queues grow without bound. Cool costs idle capacity but absorbs bursts. Batch and async work can run at 90 %+; user-facing work at 70–80 % peak.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Wait factor 1 / 2.3 / 9 / 19 ρ = 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9 / 0.95 derived; computed 24 Nov 2026
p99, M/M/1, 10 ms service 92 ms at 0.5, 461 ms at 0.9 ln(100) / (μ − λ) derived; computed 24 Nov 2026
Planning target, latency-sensitive 70–80 % peak where the curve bends default (as of Nov 2026): Google SRE book

Pitfalls

  • "Latency grows linearly with load"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: at low load, it roughly does.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: wait time grows as ρ / (1 − ρ): 90 % busy is 9× the queueing of 50 %, not 1.8×.
    ↳ Think instead: find the knee on a chart and plan below it.
  • Don't measure utilisation only on CPU.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default autoscaling metric.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the real bottleneck is a pool, a lock or connections, which saturates while CPU looks idle.
    ↳ Do instead: find the scarce resource and measure its occupancy.
  • Not the same: throughput vs utilisation
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both rise with load.
    ↳ Difference: throughput is completed work per second; utilisation is the busy fraction. Past 100 % utilisation, throughput stops growing and queues grow instead.
    ↳ Think instead: capacity is where throughput flattens.
  • "Mean latency is enough to plan with"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: Little's Law uses the mean.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the tail grows with the same factor but from a higher base, so users feel p99 long before the mean moves.
    ↳ Think instead: plan concurrency on the mean, SLOs on the tail.
  • Shelf life: both formulas are permanent; autoscaling targets move.

Connections

Path:poolingqueueing theorytail latencycapacity planning
  • Builds on latency, bandwidth, throughput.
  • Owned elsewhere: shedding owns what to do past capacity.
  • Breaks when combined with unbounded queues, which turn overload into latency instead of errors.
  • Bounded by variability: the more variable the work, the earlier the knee.

notes.title: Tail Latency — Fan-Out Makes Every Child's p99 the Parent's Median
notes.html:
References

Dean & Barroso: The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013) · gRPC: Request hedging (gRFC A6) · Gil Tene: How NOT to measure latency · Marc Brooker: Tail latency might matter more than you think

TL;DR

A request that fans out to n children waits for the slowest. If each child is slow 1 % of the time, the parent is slow 1 − 0.99ⁿ of the time: 10 % at n = 10, 26 % at 30, 63 % at 100. So in a fan-out system the children's p99 is the parent's normal experience, and one page that makes 30 calls feels everyone's tail.

Three fixes:

  • Shrink the tail at its sources: GC, queueing, noisy neighbours.
  • Hedge: after a short delay, send a duplicate to another replica and take the first answer.
  • Fan out less.

Percentiles don't add or average, so the only honest number is end-to-end.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:parent requestfan out to 30 children29 answer in ~10 msone hits a GC pause, 200 msparent waits 200 mswith hedging: after 15 ms, a duplicate to another replicaanswer at ~25 ms

Recall

Prompt Answer
Fan-out to 100, each child slow 1 %: parent slow how often? 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63 %.
What is a hedged request? A duplicate sent after a short delay; the first response wins.
What is a tied request? Two copies queued at two servers; the one that starts first cancels the other.
Can you average p99s across hosts? No. Percentiles don't average or add; merge histograms instead.
Which percentile does a user feel? With n calls per page, roughly the per-call p(1 − 1/n).
Draw by hand: fan-out a parent box with 30 arrows to children, one child red with "200 ms GC"; parent latency = the red one; then a dashed hedge arrow at 15 ms to a twin replica.

The idea

A search service's leaf servers have a p99 of 200 ms and a median of 10 ms; every team dashboard is green. The search front end queries 30 leaves per request. Its own median is 12 ms, but 45 % of requests take 200 ms, because almost half of all queries touch at least one leaf having a bad moment. Nothing is broken; the slow 2 % of leaf calls became the experience of almost half the users.

Hedging fixes it cheaply: send a second copy to another replica of any leaf that hasn't answered in 15 ms. Only about 2 % of calls trigger a hedge, and the parent's slow share falls to about 1 %.

The trade: hedging and tail work make fan-out systems fast for almost everyone, and you pay with a few percent of extra load, duplicated work unless requests are cancelled, and hedges that must be safe to repeat.

How it works

Why the parent sees the child's tail.

Children n Parent slow if any child is slow, 1 − 0.99ⁿ
1 1 %
10 10 %
30 26 %
100 63 %
Fix Cost Gain
hedge at the child's p95 ~5 % more load most tail calls replaced by a fast twin
tied requests (cancel on start) cross-server cancellation hedging without duplicated work
reduce fan-out (bigger shards, caching) data-layout work fewer chances to hit a tail
shrink the tail (GC tuning, isolation, lower ρ) engineering, spare capacity every caller benefits 
P(parent slow) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ                  ← p = 0.01, n = 100: 63 %
child tail needed for 10 % parent slow at n = 100: p ≈ 0.001 → a p99.9 target, not p99

Evolution

Lineage:2008 Google's search fan-out at scaleFeb 2013 Dean & Barroso, "The Tail at Scale"2015 HdrHistogram and coordinated-omission awareness2018 gRPC hedging policy (gRFC A6)2020s hedged reads in databases and object stores (e.g. Cassandra speculative retry)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: LLM agent workflows fan out to tools and models whose tails are seconds, not milliseconds, so the same arithmetic hits harder.
  • What won't change: the slowest child sets the parent's latency.

On the wire

A gRPC hedging policy, with the defaults that bite:

{
  "methodConfig": [{
    "name": [{ "service": "search.Leaf", "method": "Query" }],
    "hedgingPolicy": {
      "maxAttempts": 2,
      "hedgingDelay": "0.015s",
      "nonFatalStatusCodes": ["UNAVAILABLE"]
    }
  }],
  "retryThrottling": { "maxTokens": 10, "tokenRatio": 0.1 }
}

hedgingDelay sits near the child's p95, so only the slowest ~5 % hedge. The defaults that bite: a delay of 0s sends every request twice; hedging a non-idempotent method duplicates its effect; and without retryThrottling, hedges keep firing during an overload.

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): 30 children per request, each 8–12 ms with a 2 % chance of a 200 ms stall, 50,000 parent requests.

def child(): return 200.0 if random() < 0.02 else uniform(8, 12)
def parent(n, hedge=None):
    times = []
    for _ in range(n):
        t = child()
        if hedge and t > hedge: t = min(t, hedge + child())   # duplicate to another replica
        times.append(t)
    return max(times)
# look for: share of parents slower than 100 ms, and extra load
# naive belief predicts: a 2 % child problem is a 2 % user problem

Run: without hedging, 45.0 % of parents take over 100 ms (p95 200 ms). Hedging at 15 ms brings it to 1.2 % (p95 27 ms) for 2.0 % more child calls.

Measure it

  • See it: a histogram of parent latency next to child latency, and the fan-out count per request from traces.
  • In production: end-to-end p99 and p99.9 from merged histograms (HdrHistogram, OpenTelemetry exponential histograms), hedge rate and hedge win rate, per-child p99.9.
  • Bounded by: queueing at the children → queueing theory; hedges as load → retry budgets.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: In fan-out, the parent waits for the slowest child, so the parent's slow rate is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ: 63 % at 100 children with a 1 % tail each. So children need p99.9 targets. I shrink tail sources, reduce fan-out, and hedge: a duplicate after about the child's p95, first answer wins, for a few percent extra load. And I measure end-to-end from merged histograms, because percentiles don't average.

Q · Mechanism — Why do hedged requests cost only a few percent of load? The duplicate is sent only if the first copy hasn't answered by the hedging delay. With the delay at the child's p95, about 5 % of calls hedge, so load rises about 5 %. Since tail stalls are mostly independent across replicas (a GC pause on one host), the twin usually answers at normal speed.

Q · Trade-off — Hedging or tied requests? Hedging is simple and client-only, but the slow copy keeps doing work after the fast one wins. Tied requests enqueue at two servers that know about each other; the first to start work cancels its twin, so almost no work is duplicated. Hedging when calls are cheap and idempotent; tied requests when the work is expensive and servers support cancellation.

Q · Failure — Every service's p99 meets its SLO, but users complain of slowness. Why? Two errors at once. A page makes many calls, so users feel roughly the per-call p(1 − 1/n), well past p99. And the dashboard may average p99s across hosts, which hides bad ones. Measure end-to-end page latency from merged histograms, and set child SLOs from the fan-out.

Q · Design — Tail-latency strategy for an agent that calls 8 tools in parallel per step.

  • Budget: per-step deadline; each tool call gets it as a deadline, not a fixed timeout.
  • Hedging: for idempotent read tools, hedge at the tool's p95 with a budget.
  • Partial results: return with the tools that answered, flagging the missing one, rather than waiting for the slowest.
  • Measure: per-step latency histograms and per-tool p99.9.

Compare

No mitigation Hedged requests Tied requests
Parent slow share (model) 45 % 1.2 % about the same as hedging
Extra load 0 ~2–5 % near 0 (twin cancelled)
Needs nothing idempotent calls, a budget server-side cancellation
Duplicate work none the slow copy finishes cancelled on start

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Parent slow rate, n = 100, p = 1 % 63 % 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ spec (as of Nov 2026): Dean & Barroso 2013
Child tail for 10 % parent slow at n = 100 p ≈ 0.001 a p99.9 target derived
Model: 30 children, 2 % stalls 45 % → 1.2 % slow with hedging +2 % load derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Hedge at the child's p95 ~5 % extra load only slow calls hedge spec (as of Nov 2026): Dean & Barroso 2013

Pitfalls

  • "Our p99 is fine, so users are fine"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: p99 sounds like "almost everyone".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a page with 30 calls hits at least one p99 on 26 % of loads; users live in your tail.
    ↳ Think instead: set child targets from fan-out: p99.9 at n = 100.
  • "Average the p99s across hosts for the fleet p99"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's one query over existing metrics.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: percentiles don't average; one bad host vanishes into the mean and the result matches no real request.
    ↳ Think instead: merge histograms, then take the percentile.
  • Don't hedge with a zero delay or no budget.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: hedging immediately gives the lowest latency.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every call doubles, and during overload hedges add load where it hurts most.
    ↳ Do instead: delay at the child's p95, plus a throttling budget.
  • Not the same: a hedge vs a retry
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both send the request again.
    ↳ Difference: a retry follows a failure and replaces the first attempt; a hedge races a still-running attempt.
    ↳ Think instead: retry for errors, hedge for slowness; both need idempotency.
  • Don't measure latency with a closed-loop load generator alone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's how most benchmark tools work by default.
    ↳ What goes wrong: when the server stalls, the generator stops sending, so the stall is recorded once instead of for every request that would have arrived (coordinated omission).
    ↳ Do instead: an open-loop, constant-rate generator, or correct for the omission.
  • Shelf life: fan-out arithmetic is permanent; hedging APIs and histogram formats move.

Connections

Path:queueing theorytail latencyhead-of-line blockingcapacity planning
  • Builds on where latency goes.
  • Owned elsewhere: metrics that matter owns histogram practice; retries owns budgets.
  • Breaks when combined with non-idempotent hedges or unbudgeted hedging.
  • Bounded by fan-out: the more children, the rarer each child's tail must be.

notes.title: Head-of-Line Blocking — One Idea in Four Places: TCP, HTTP/1.1, Queues, Worker Pools
notes.html:
References

RFC 9000: QUIC, §2 streams · RFC 9113: HTTP/2, §5 streams and multiplexing · Daniel Stenberg: HTTP/3 explained, TCP head-of-line blocking · Amazon Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

TL;DR

Head-of-line (HOL) blocking: one item at the front of an ordered line holds up everything behind it, however ready they are. The same shape shows up in four places, with four fixes:

Where The blocking item Fix
TCP a lost segment; later bytes wait for its retransmission QUIC: independent streams
HTTP/1.1 a slow response on the connection HTTP/2 multiplexing, or more connections
a message queue a poison or slow message at the head dead-letter queue, parallel partitions
a worker pool slow requests holding every worker separate pools per request class
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:8 workers, FIFOa burst of 1-second requests takes all 810 ms requests queue behind themfast p99 becomes 106 mssplit into a fast pool and a slow poolfast p99 back to 10 ms

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where does HTTP/2 fix HOL blocking, and where not? It fixes it at HTTP; TCP still delivers in order, so one loss stalls every stream.
What does QUIC change? Loss recovery per stream: a loss stalls only its own stream.
The worker-pool version? Slow requests occupy every worker; cheap requests wait behind them.

The idea

An API's p99 for a 10 ms endpoint is 106 ms, though nothing about that endpoint changed. A report endpoint that takes 1 s shares the same 8-worker pool. Whenever a few reports arrive together they take most of the workers, and the fast requests queue behind them. The fast endpoint isn't slow; it's waiting in line.

The trade: a single ordered line is simple and fair in arrival order, and you pay when work items differ in size, because the big ones set the wait for everyone behind them.

How it works

The worker-pool case, modelled on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): 8 workers, 60 rps, 95 % of requests take 10 ms and 5 % take 1 s, 40,000 requests.

Layout Fast requests p50 Fast requests p99
one FIFO pool of 8 10 ms 106 ms
fast pool of 4 + slow pool of 4 10 ms 10 ms

The cost of splitting: the slow pool runs at about 75 % busy (3 rps × 1 s over 4 workers), so slow requests now queue more. Isolation moves the wait onto the class that causes it.

TCP:   one lost segment ─▶ receiver holds later bytes ─▶ every HTTP/2 stream waits one RTO or RTT
QUIC:  one lost packet  ─▶ only the stream whose frames it carried waits

Evolution

Lineage:1981 TCP in-order delivery1997 HTTP/1.1 pipelining, which nobody could deploy because of HOL2015 HTTP/2 multiplexing2021 QUIC (RFC 9000)2022 HTTP/3
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: HTTP/3 is served by most CDNs; the transport case is solved where QUIC is allowed through.
  • What won't change: any single ordered line with mixed sizes blocks.

On the wire

Splitting a worker pool by request class in nginx, with the default that bites:

upstream api_fast    { server 10.0.1.10:8080; }   # 4 app workers listening here
upstream api_reports { server 10.0.1.10:8081; }   # 4 separate workers for slow work
location /reports/ { proxy_pass http://api_reports; proxy_read_timeout 30s; }
location /         { proxy_pass http://api_fast;    proxy_read_timeout 2s; }
# the default that bites: one gunicorn/uvicorn worker pool for every route, so the slowest route sets everyone's queue

Measure it

  • See it: queue time per request (time from accept to start of handling) split by endpoint; a fast endpoint with high queue time is blocked behind something.
  • In production: per-class latency, worker occupancy by route, TCP retransmits next to HTTP/2 stream stalls, queue age of the oldest message.
  • Bounded by: transport → HTTP/2's remaining flaw and QUIC; pools → bulkheads.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Head-of-line blocking is one item at the front of an ordered line stalling everything behind it. HTTP/1.1 has it per connection, HTTP/2 fixed that but TCP still has it on loss, and QUIC fixes it per stream. The same thing happens in queues with a poison message and in worker pools where slow requests hold every worker. The general fix is separate lines for work of different sizes.

Q · Mechanism — Why does HTTP/2 over TCP suffer under packet loss? HTTP/2 puts every stream on one TCP connection. TCP delivers bytes in order, so when one segment is lost the kernel holds every later byte, whatever stream it belongs to, until the retransmission arrives. At 1–2 % loss, HTTP/2 can do worse than several HTTP/1.1 connections, each of which stalls alone.

Q · Trade-off — Separate pools per request class, or one larger pool? One larger pool uses capacity better on average but lets slow work starve fast work. Separate pools isolate classes but leave capacity idle in one while the other queues. Separate when classes differ by 10× or more in cost and the fast class has a tight SLO; one pool when work is uniform.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Fast-request p99, one pool vs split 106 ms vs 10 ms 8 workers, 5 % of requests 1 s derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Slow pool utilisation after the split ~75 % 3 rps × 1 s / 4 workers derived
HTTP/2 streams per TCP connection default 100 concurrent (common servers) one loss stalls all of them default (as of Nov 2026): nginx http2_max_concurrent_streams

Pitfalls

  • "HTTP/2 solved head-of-line blocking"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the headline feature of multiplexing.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it moved the blocking to TCP, where one lost segment stalls every stream on the connection.
    ↳ Think instead: HTTP/2 fixes the application layer; QUIC fixes the transport.
  • Don't share one worker pool between fast and slow routes.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one pool is simpler and uses capacity well.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the slow route sets the queue for every route, and fast endpoints miss their SLOs for no visible reason.
    ↳ Do instead: a pool per class when costs differ by an order of magnitude.
  • Not the same: HOL blocking vs slow processing
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both show as high latency on the slow-looking endpoint.
    ↳ Difference: slow processing is time spent working; HOL blocking is time spent waiting behind other work.
    ↳ Think instead: split queue time from service time in every latency metric.
  • "A poison message just fails once"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: errors are usually transient.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in an ordered queue it's redelivered at the head forever, blocking every message behind it.
    ↳ Think instead: a retry limit and a dead-letter queue.
  • Shelf life: the idea is permanent; which layers still have it changes as QUIC spreads.

Connections

Path:tail latencyhead-of-line blockingidempotency
  • Builds on TCP head-of-line blocking and HTTP/1.1 limits.
  • Owned elsewhere: QUIC owns per-stream loss recovery.
