  • Breaks when combined with one shared pool for work of very different sizes.
  • Bounded by queueing theory: variability lengthens every queue.

notes.title: Idempotency & the Exactly-Once Delusion — At-Least-Once Plus Dedup Is the Real Answer
notes.html:
References

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent methods · IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP header field · Stripe: Idempotent requests · Kafka: Exactly-once semantics (transactions)

TL;DR

Across a network, a sender can't tell a lost request from a lost reply. Both look like silence. So it can only choose:

  • At-most-once: never resend, and sometimes lose work.
  • At-least-once: resend until acknowledged, and sometimes deliver twice.

"Exactly once" isn't something a network delivers. It's an effect you build: at-least-once delivery plus a receiver that recognises repeats. An idempotency key does that. The client attaches a unique key; the server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result for any repeat.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:client creates key kPOST /payments with Idempotency-Key: kserver: seen k?no: lock k, charge, store result under kreply lostclient retries with kserver returns the stored result, no second charge

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does idempotent mean? Repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once (the response may differ).
Why is exactly-once delivery impossible? The sender can't tell a lost request from a lost acknowledgement.
What makes a POST safe to retry? An idempotency key the server deduplicates on.

The idea

A mobile app sends "pay ₹2,000". The server charges the card and replies, but the reply dies when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to mobile data. The app sees a timeout and retries. Without a key, the customer is charged twice. With a key, the server finds the first result under that key and returns it: one charge, and the app gets its success.

Kafka's "exactly-once" is the same idea inside one system: producer IDs and sequence numbers dedup retries, and transactions commit reads and writes together. It doesn't extend to an email you sent from the consumer.

The trade: at-least-once plus dedup gives an exactly-once effect over an unreliable network, and you pay with a key store (with a retention window), a check on every write, and care for the race where two copies arrive at once.

How it works

Case Server behaviour with a key
first request with k lock k, do the work, store status and body under k
repeat after completion return the stored response; do nothing
repeat while the first is in flight 409 Conflict (or wait); never run twice
same k, different body 422: a key reused for a different request is a client bug
key older than retention (e.g. 24 h) treated as new: retention must exceed the client's retry window 
idempotent methods (RFC 9110): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE
not idempotent: POST, PATCH   → need a key, or a natural one (order ID, payment intent ID)

Evolution

Lineage:1980s RPC at-most-once vs at-least-once semantics1999 HTTP/1.1 defines idempotent methods2015 Stripe's Idempotency-Key2017 Kafka idempotent producer and transactions2021 IETF Idempotency-Key draft2022 RFC 9110
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: the IETF draft standardises the header name and error codes; payment and LLM APIs accept keys on create calls.
  • What won't change: lost request and lost reply look the same to the sender.

On the wire

Two attempts with one key, with the default that bites:

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c9e1a-2b7d-4c55-9e0a-8f1d2c3b4a5e
Content-Type: application/json

{"amount": 200000, "currency": "INR", "source": "tok_visa"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created                       ← first attempt (reply lost in transit)
HTTP/1.1 201 Created                       ← retry with the same key: same body, replayed
Idempotent-Replayed: true                  (Stripe's header for a replayed response)

The default that bites: a client that generates a new key per attempt instead of per operation gets no dedup at all.

Measure it

  • See it: send the same keyed request twice and compare: one effect in the database, two identical responses.
  • In production: replayed-response count per endpoint, 409 in-flight conflicts, key reuse with mismatched bodies (client bugs), and duplicate effects found by reconciliation.
  • Bounded by: retry policy → retries; the key contract → idempotency keys.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A sender can't distinguish a lost request from a lost reply, so the network offers at-most-once or at-least-once, never exactly-once. Exactly-once is an effect: at-least-once delivery plus a receiver that dedups. For HTTP that's an idempotency key per operation, stored with the result, and replayed on repeats. Kafka's exactly-once is the same idea within Kafka only.

Q · Mechanism — What happens if two copies with the same key arrive at the same time? Both check the store and see no result. Without a lock, both run. The server must claim the key atomically first (an insert with a unique constraint, or a conditional write), so the second copy sees "in progress" and gets 409 or waits for the first result.

Q · Trade-off — Client-generated keys or natural business keys? Client keys (UUIDs) work for any request but need a store and a retention window. Natural keys (order ID, invoice number) need no extra store, because the unique constraint on the business record is the dedup. Use natural keys where the domain has one; client keys for generic create endpoints.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Idempotent HTTP methods 6 GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 9110 §9.2.2
Stripe key retention at least 24 h keys may be pruned after default (as of Nov 2026): Stripe idempotent requests
Delivery guarantees possible end to end at-most-once or at-least-once the two-generals problem spec (as of Nov 2026): distributed-systems result

Pitfalls

  • "Our queue gives exactly-once delivery"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the product page says exactly-once.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it holds inside that system; side effects outside it (an email, a call to another API) can still repeat on redelivery.
    ↳ Think instead: make every external effect idempotent with its own key.
  • Don't generate a new key on each retry.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: keys look like request IDs, and request IDs are unique per attempt.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every retry looks new to the server, so duplicates go through.
    ↳ Do instead: one key per logical operation, kept across attempts.
  • Not the same: idempotent vs safe
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both make a method "OK to repeat".
    ↳ Difference: safe means no state change (GET); idempotent means repeats change nothing further (PUT, DELETE).
    ↳ Think instead: safe ⊂ idempotent: DELETE is idempotent but not safe.
  • "Check, then insert, is enough dedup"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works in every test that sends one request at a time.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: two concurrent copies both pass the check before either inserts.
    ↳ Think instead: claim the key atomically with a unique constraint or conditional write.
  • Shelf life: the impossibility is permanent; header names and retention conventions move.

Connections

Path:retriesidempotencydegradation and backpressure
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable.
  • Owned elsewhere: idempotency keys owns the header contract and storage design.
  • Breaks when combined with retried timeouts on unkeyed writes.
  • Bounded by key retention: a retry after the window is a new request.

notes.title: Graceful Degradation & Backpressure — Serve Less, or Ask Upstream to Send Less
notes.html:
References

Google SRE book: Addressing cascading failures, degradation · RFC 9113 §5.2: HTTP/2 flow control · Reactive Streams specification · Amazon Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

TL;DR

Two answers to "more work is arriving than I can do":

  • Graceful degradation: do less per request and still answer, with a cached price, no recommendations, a lower-quality model. A worse answer beats no answer.
  • Backpressure: tell the sender to slow down, through a full bounded buffer, a flow-control window or a 429 with Retry-After, instead of buffering silently.

The anti-pattern behind both is the unbounded buffer. It hides overload as memory growth until the process dies, and then all the buffered work is lost anyway.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:load risesstep 1: drop optional features (recommendations)step 2: serve stale cachestep 3: cheaper model or fewer resultsstep 4: shed with 429 and Retry-Afterupstream slows download fallssteps undone in reverse

Recall

Prompt Answer
Degradation vs shedding? Degradation serves a worse answer; shedding serves none.
What is backpressure? The slow consumer signalling the producer to send less.
Where does HTTP/2 implement it? Per-stream and per-connection flow-control windows.

The idea

A shopping site's product page calls price, stock, reviews and recommendations. During a sale, recommendations slows to seconds. A site without a plan waits, and the whole page times out. A site with a degradation ladder drops recommendations first, then serves reviews from yesterday's cache, and keeps price and stock live. Customers see a plainer page and can still buy.

The same sale floods an order-event consumer. If it buffers in memory, it crashes after an hour and loses everything in the buffer. If its queue is bounded, producers block or get 429s, and the backlog stays in a durable queue where it can drain later.

The trade: degradation and backpressure keep the core working under overload, and you pay with deciding in advance what is optional, and with producers that must handle "slow down" instead of assuming infinite capacity.

How it works

A degradation ladder: each step has a trigger, an action and a cost.

Step Trigger Action User sees
1 p99 of an optional dependency > 300 ms skip it (breaker open) no recommendations
2 database CPU > 75 % serve reads from cache, stale up to 5 min slightly old reviews
3 GPU queue > 2 s smaller model, shorter answers simpler answers
4 concurrency limit reached 429 + Retry-After for low-priority traffic "try again shortly"

Backpressure, by transport:

Transport Signal Default that bites
TCP receive window shrinks to 0 app reads into an unbounded queue, so TCP never sees the pressure
HTTP/2 stream window not replenished servers raise windows to MBs, so buffers grow before pressure shows
queue consumer bounded in-memory buffer blocks unbounded asyncio.Queue() or channel
HTTP API 429 / 503 with Retry-After clients ignore Retry-After and retry at once

Evolution

Lineage:1981 TCP receive window2011 Netflix fallbacks in Hystrix2015 Reactive Streams and HTTP/2 flow control2016 Google SRE book: degradation modes2020s model fallbacks (smaller model under load) in LLM serving
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: AI products degrade by model tier and output length; gateways shed by request priority.
  • What won't change: a buffer without a bound only delays the failure.

On the wire

A bounded consumer in Python 3.15, with the default that bites:

queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1000)   # default maxsize=0 means UNBOUNDED: memory grows until OOM
async def on_event(event):
    try:
        queue.put_nowait(event)       # full → we push back instead of buffering forever
    except asyncio.QueueFull:
        raise TooBusy(retry_after=5)  # surfaced to the producer as 429 + Retry-After: 5

Measure it

  • See it: process memory and queue depth under a load test past capacity: an unbounded buffer shows a ramp to OOM; a bounded one stays flat with rising rejections.
  • In production: current degradation step per service, fallback rate per feature, queue depth and age of the oldest item, 429 rate and whether clients honour Retry-After.
  • Bounded by: shedding → breakers and shedding; streaming backpressure → backpressure in streams.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Under overload I want to keep the core working. Degradation answers with less: drop optional features, serve stale cache, cheaper models, in a planned ladder. Backpressure makes producers slow down: bounded buffers, flow-control windows, 429 with Retry-After. The anti-pattern is an unbounded buffer, which converts overload into memory growth and then a crash.

Q · Mechanism — How does backpressure travel through a TCP connection? The receiving app stops reading; the kernel's receive buffer fills; TCP advertises a smaller window, down to zero; the sender's send buffer fills; the sender's write blocks. That works end to end only if every hop reads only as fast as it can process. One unbounded queue in the middle absorbs the pressure and breaks the chain.

Q · Trade-off — Degrade or shed? Degrading keeps every user served at lower quality, but needs fallbacks built in advance, and some work can't degrade (a payment either happens or it doesn't). Shedding is simple and always available but gives some users nothing. Degrade optional features first; shed only when the core itself is past capacity, lowest priority first.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
HTTP/2 initial stream window 65,535 bytes raised by most servers spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 9113 §6.9.2
asyncio.Queue default maxsize 0 (unbounded) the default that bites default (as of Nov 2026): Python docs
Ladder steps 4 features, cache, model, shed illustrative

Pitfalls

  • "A bigger buffer absorbs the spike"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: spikes are short and buffers are cheap.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: if the spike outlasts the buffer, it only delays the failure and adds latency to everything inside.
    ↳ Think instead: bound buffers at what drains within the deadline, then push back.
  • Don't design degradation during the incident.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: nobody knows in advance which feature will fail.
    ↳ What goes wrong: under pressure, people turn off the wrong thing or nothing at all.
    ↳ Do instead: a written ladder with triggers, tested in game days.
  • Not the same: backpressure vs rate limiting
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both make the sender slow down.
    ↳ Difference: rate limiting is a fixed quota per client; backpressure reflects the receiver's current capacity, whatever the quota.
    ↳ Think instead: quota for fairness, backpressure for capacity.
  • "Clients will honour Retry-After"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's in the HTTP spec, and your own client honours it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: many third-party clients and SDKs retry immediately, turning each 429 into more load.
    ↳ Think instead: verify client behaviour and enforce with budgets.
  • Shelf life: bounded buffers and ladders are durable; transport window defaults and SDK behaviour move.

Connections

Path:breakers and sheddingdegradation and backpressurecascading failures
  • Builds on TCP flow control.
  • Owned elsewhere: backpressure in streams owns WebSocket and SSE cases; rate limiting owns quotas.
  • Breaks when combined with one unbounded queue anywhere in the chain.
  • Bounded by what the product can live without: degradation needs optional parts.

notes.title: Cascading Failures & Thundering Herds — When the Failure Generates Its Own Load
notes.html:
References

Google SRE book: Addressing cascading failures · Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter · Vattani et al.: Optimal probabilistic cache stampede prevention (VLDB 2015) · AWS: Summary of the us-east-1 event, Dec 2021

TL;DR

A failure cascades when it creates load that makes it worse: a positive feedback loop. The common loops:

  • Retry storms: failures cause retries, which cause more failures.
  • Cache stampedes: one hot key expires, and every request misses at once.
  • Death spirals: losing one instance pushes its load onto the others until they fail too.
  • Health-check flapping: overloaded instances fail checks, leave the pool, and the rest get more load.

The signature on a graph: request rate rising while success rate falls, with flat user traffic. Only removing load breaks the loop. Adding capacity rarely wins, because new instances start cold into the same storm.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:one instance slowsits requests time outcallers retrythe other instances get more loadthey slowhealth checks failinstances leave the poolsurvivors get even morewhole service down

Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes a failure cascade? Positive feedback: the failure creates load that deepens the failure.
The graph signature? Requests up, successes down, users flat.
The one thing that breaks the loop? Removing load: shed, break, throttle retries.

The idea

A cache in front of a database holds a popular product's page for 60 s. At second 60 it expires, and 2,000 requests in that same second all miss and query the database together. The database, sized for the 1 % that normally misses, slows; the queries time out; callers retry; the cache never gets refilled because the refill query keeps timing out. One expiry became an outage.

Recovery is often harder than the failure. When the database comes back, every queued retry and every cold cache arrives in the same second.

The trade: shared caches, pools and retries make normal operation efficient, and you pay with feedback loops that can turn a small fault into a full outage unless each loop has a breaker built in.

How it works

Loop Trigger Breaker for the loop
retry storm errors → retries → more errors retry budgets, one retrying layer (retries)
cache stampede hot key expires → N misses at once request coalescing (one refill per key), early random refresh, serve stale
death spiral one instance lost → load moves to the rest headroom for N−1, shedding at each instance
health-check flapping overload → failed checks → fewer instances checks that ignore load; never eject more than a cap (e.g. 50 %)
synchronized clients timers, cron, reconnects at the same moment jitter on every timer and backoff 
stampede load = request rate × refill time      ← 2,000 rps × 1 s refill = 2,000 identical DB queries
with coalescing = 1 query per key per refill
N−1 headroom: survivors carry N / (N − 1) of normal load   ← 3 instances → each at 1.5×

Evolution

Lineage:1990s "thundering herd" in Unix accept() wakeups2010 Facebook's memcache leases2015 probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)2016 Google SRE book: cascading failuresDec 2021 AWS us-east-1 event: internal retry storms named in the summary
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: CDNs and caches coalesce requests by default (request collapsing); meshes cap outlier ejection.
  • What won't change: any loop where failure creates load needs a deliberate break.

On the wire

Request coalescing in nginx, with the default that bites:

proxy_cache_lock on;              # default off: every miss for a key goes to the origin at once
proxy_cache_lock_timeout 5s;
proxy_cache_use_stale updating error timeout;   # serve the old copy while one request refreshes
proxy_cache_background_update on;

Measure it

  • See it: request rate, success rate and user-facing traffic on one graph; a widening gap between requests and users is retry load.
  • In production: retries per user request, cache hit rate per hot key, healthy-instance count vs ejected, origin queries per cache miss (should be 1 with coalescing).
  • Bounded by: load removal → shedding and breakers; sizing for N−1 → capacity planning.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A cascade is positive feedback: failure creates load that deepens the failure. Retry storms, cache stampedes, death spirals and health-check flapping are the usual loops. The signature is requests rising while successes fall and users stay flat. The fix is removing load (shed, open breakers, budget retries), coalescing cache refills, jitter everywhere, and N−1 headroom, then ramping traffic back slowly.

Q · Mechanism — Why does adding capacity during a cascade often fail? New instances start cold (empty caches, no JIT, empty pools) and join while retries are at their peak. They get the full storm at their slowest, fail health checks, and leave. Shed load first so the system stabilises, then add capacity and ramp traffic.

Q · Trade-off — Short cache TTLs or long ones with stale serving? Short TTLs keep data fresh but expire hot keys often, inviting stampedes. Long TTLs with serve-stale-while-refresh give one background refresh per key and survive origin outages, at the cost of staleness. Serve stale with coalesced refresh for read-heavy data; short TTLs only where staleness is unacceptable.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Stampede, 2,000 rps, 1 s refill 2,000 origin queries vs 1 with coalescing derived
Survivor load after losing 1 of 3 1.5× N / (N − 1) derived
nginx proxy_cache_lock off every miss reaches the origin default (as of Nov 2026): nginx proxy module

Pitfalls

  • "More capacity fixes an outage"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: overload looks like too little capacity.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: new instances join cold into the retry storm and fail, while the loop keeps feeding itself.
    ↳ Think instead: remove load first, then add capacity and ramp slowly.
  • Don't let health checks eject the whole pool.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: unhealthy instances shouldn't get traffic.
    ↳ What goes wrong: under overload every instance fails, the pool empties, and nothing serves at all.
    ↳ Do instead: cap ejection (e.g. at 50 %) and keep load out of liveness checks.
  • Not the same: thundering herd vs retry storm
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are sudden synchronized load.
    ↳ Difference: a herd is many clients triggered by one event (an expiry, a restart); a storm is load multiplied by failures.
    ↳ Think instead: jitter and coalescing for herds, budgets for storms.
  • "Recovery is the easy part"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the root cause is fixed, so traffic should flow again.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: queued retries, reconnects and cold caches all arrive at the same moment of restore.
    ↳ Think instead: restore traffic gradually, behind shedding.
  • Shelf life: the loops are permanent; cache and mesh defaults move.

Connections

Path:degradation and backpressurecascading failurescapacity planning
  • Builds on retries and HTTP caching.
  • Owned elsewhere: probes owns probe design; outlier detection owns ejection caps.
  • Breaks when combined with unbudgeted retries, synchronized timers or unlocked caches.
  • Bounded by headroom: a system at 95 % has no room to absorb any loop.

notes.title: Capacity Planning — Requests, Concurrency, Bandwidth and the Connection Ceilings
notes.html:
References

Google SRE book: Software engineering in SRE, capacity planning · AWS: NAT gateway limits · AWS: ALB quotas · Google SRE workbook: Managing load

TL;DR

Size four dimensions, because any one can bind first:

  • Requests per second at peak: the daily average × the peak-to-average ratio.
  • Concurrency: Little's Law, peak rps × latency.
  • Bandwidth: peak rps × response size.
  • Connection ceilings: NAT ports per destination, file descriptors, LB and proxy limits. These bind first on streaming workloads.

Plan for ~70 % of the bottleneck at peak and for losing one AZ, because queueing explodes past the knee and a lost zone moves its load onto the rest.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:requests per dayaverage rps× peak ratioconcurrency (λW), bandwidth (λ × size), connections÷ per-instance capacity at 70 %× N / (N − 1) for an AZ losscheck every ceiling

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four dimensions? Peak rps, concurrency, bandwidth, connection ceilings.
Concurrency from throughput? L = λW: 1,389 rps × 80 ms ≈ 111.
What utilisation do you plan to? ~70 % of the bottleneck at peak, after losing one AZ.

The idea

A team sizes a new service from its average load and gets 3 instances. Launch day brings 3× the average at the evening peak, one AZ has a bad hour, and the service falls over. Average load was never the number that mattered: peak load, divided by the capacity left after a zone loss, at a utilisation where queues stay short.

The trade: planning for peak, N−1 and 70 % costs idle capacity most of the day, and you pay for it in exchange for latency that holds at peak and a zone loss that isn't an outage.

How it works

A worked plan: 40 million requests a day, peak 3× average, 80 ms latency, 40 kB responses, 250 rps per instance at 100 % busy, 3 AZs. Computed with Python 3.15 on 24 Nov 2026.

Dimension Formula Value
average rps 40 M / 86,400 463
peak rps × 3 1,389
concurrency at peak 1,389 × 0.080 s ≈ 111 in flight
egress at peak 1,389 × 40 kB × 8 ≈ 444 Mbit/s
instances at 70 % ⌈1,389 / (250 × 0.7)⌉ 8
instances surviving an AZ loss ⌈8 × 3 / 2⌉ 12
Ceiling Typical limit Binds when
NAT gateway 55,000 connections per destination per IP many pods call one external API
ephemeral ports 28,232 per (src, dst IP, port) no pooling (pooling)
file descriptors ulimit -n, often 1,024 by default long-lived WebSockets or SSE
proxy workers nginx worker_connections 512 by default each proxied request uses two

Evolution

Lineage:1917 Erlang's trunk sizing1961 Little's Law2006 elastic cloud capacity2016 Google SRE book: N+2 and intent-based planning2020s autoscaling on queue depth and custom metrics
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: GPU and token-based capacity (tokens per second, KV-cache memory) joins rps as a dimension for AI workloads.
  • What won't change: peak, headroom and the slowest-growing ceiling decide the plan.

On the wire

Checking the connection ceilings on a host, with the defaults that bite:

ulimit -n                               # 1024 on many distros: 1,024 WebSockets and you're done
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range     # 32768 60999 → 28,232 ports per destination
ss -s                                   # TCP: estab, timewait — compare against both limits
# nginx: worker_connections defaults to 512 per worker, and a proxied request holds two

Measure it

  • See it: a load test to the knee: plot p99 against rps and mark where it bends; that's per-instance capacity, not the vendor number.
  • In production: peak-to-average ratio per week, utilisation of the bottleneck at peak, headroom after the largest AZ, and each ceiling's current use (NAT ErrorPortAllocation, fds, LB connections).
  • Bounded by: queueing → queueing theory; NAT and egress → IGW, NAT and egress.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I size four things: peak rps from daily volume and the peak ratio, concurrency by Little's Law, bandwidth from response size, and connection ceilings like NAT ports, file descriptors and proxy limits. I plan the bottleneck at about 70 % at peak with one AZ lost, and I get per-instance capacity from a load test to the knee, not a spec sheet.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a lost AZ need more than a third more capacity? With 3 zones, each carries a third. Lose one and the other two carry half each: 1.5× their normal load. If they were at 70 %, they're now at 105 %, past capacity. So you plan at 70 % after the loss, which means about 47 % in normal times.

Q · Trade-off — Overprovision or autoscale? Autoscaling saves money on average but reacts in minutes, starts instances cold and can't help with spikes shorter than its reaction time. Overprovisioning absorbs spikes instantly but pays for idle capacity. Keep a base that survives an AZ loss at peak, and autoscale above it on queue depth.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Worked plan 8 instances, 12 with an AZ loss 40 M req/day, 3× peak, 250 rps each derived; computed 24 Nov 2026
NAT gateway connections 55,000 per destination per IP simultaneous default (as of Nov 2026): AWS NAT gateway docs
nginx worker_connections 512 per worker default (as of Nov 2026): nginx core module

Pitfalls

  • "Size for the average and let autoscaling handle peaks"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: average is what you pay for most of the day.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: peaks arrive faster than instances start, and new instances start cold.
    ↳ Think instead: base capacity for peak with an AZ lost; autoscale above it.
  • Don't plan from CPU alone.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the metric every dashboard leads with.
    ↳ What goes wrong: streaming and proxy workloads hit file descriptors, ports or NAT limits at 20 % CPU.
    ↳ Do instead: list every ceiling and its current use.
  • Not the same: vendor capacity vs measured capacity
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "rps per instance".
    ↳ Difference: vendor numbers come from ideal payloads; yours comes from a load test with real requests to the latency knee.
    ↳ Think instead: load-test to the knee and plan from that.
  • "Bandwidth is never the limit"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: cloud networks are fast.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: instances have per-instance bandwidth caps and NAT gateways have throughput limits; large responses hit them before CPU.
    ↳ Think instead: compute peak rps × size and compare.
  • Shelf life: the method is durable; instance, NAT and LB limits move.

Connections

Path:queueing theorycapacity planningmetrics that matter
  • Builds on IGW, NAT and egress for NAT limits.
  • Owned elsewhere: pooling owns port exhaustion.
  • Breaks when combined with an AZ loss at planned utilisation above ~47 %.
  • Bounded by cascading failures: no headroom means no recovery.
